Article: Brotli2Shell: Beyond Node(2Shell) and HTTP(2Shell)
Source: https://research.jfrog.com/post/brotli2shell-beyond-node2shell-and-http2shell/

Evidence and artifact identity
- Read saved article.txt and the original HTML recovered with Forager.
- article-links.txt and article-images.json enumerate the original page's links
  and images. Downloaded and inspected all five research screenshots in images/.
  The HTML contains no preformatted code blocks; the actual API snippet and
  commands are in screenshots. article-code.txt is consequently empty.
- Screenshot 1: curl --data-binary @payload.br -H "Content-Encoding: br"
  http://clickhouse:8123/ followed by signal 11, BrotliDecoderStateCleanup,
  and DB::BrotliReadBuffer::~BrotliReadBuffer(). Tested ClickHouse 26.10.2.103.
- Screenshot 2: FFmpeg/libjxl receives malformed JPEG XL metadata; ASan reports
  a free through a pointer containing 0x41 bytes. The article specifies the
  JPEG XL signature, ftyp, brob(Exif + malicious Brotli), and real jxlc image.
- Screenshot 3: .NET 10.0.13 (vendored Brotli 1.1.0), staged native decoding,
  first-stage 23,068,693 bytes, second-stage 127-byte overflow, SIGSEGV.
- Screenshot 4: pyarrow 26.0.0, vendored Brotli 1.0.9:
  pa.Codec("brotli").decompress(open("dos-tail.br", "rb").read(),
                               decompressed_size=64*1024*1024)
  The 534-byte input hangs; patched Brotli 1.2.1 rejects it.
- Screenshot 5 shows contextual scanner findings for ordinary Express/body-parser
  calls. These are exposure evidence, not malicious behavior by themselves.
- Forager fetched the linked JFrog scanner, upstream fix, and Arrow/.NET issues.
  These provide context but no downloadable original JFrog exploit files.
  Their HTML and .forage.json provenance remain under context/generic/.
- The article's published vector is
  200010414141fcffff07002228f00b60f7f41f000000.
  Parsed its first header: WBITS=16, non-final, MLEN=2 (three bytes),
  ISUNCOMPRESSED=1. Thus 414141 is attacker-controlled literal content, not a
  fixed protocol marker. The following maximum-sized compressed meta-block
  and invalid block switch form the attack structure. The rule masks only
  those three literal bytes and omits trailing padding.
- testdata/suspicious/jxl_metadata_builder.py is a representative reconstruction
  of the described technique, NOT the original unpublished PoC.
- Reconstructed a 214-byte container as reconstructed.jxl to verify the builder:
  signature box 12 bytes, ftyp 20 bytes, brob 34 bytes, jxlc 148 bytes.
  The 140-byte real codestream comes from libjxl's clean 1x1_exif_xmp.jxl test
  image recovered by Forager. It is comparison material, not an IOC.
  No vulnerable decoder or exploit was executed.
- The article's HTML .forage.json remains in downloads/ outside the acceptance
  sample set; all provenance is excluded from that sample set.

Placement and generalization
- New objectives/execution/exploit/brotli-block-switch is a mechanism leaf for
  constructing malformed Brotli block-switch inputs. This is memory corruption
  through an invalid decoder state transition, distinct from generic buffer
  operations, resource-exhaustion loops, and ordinary decompression APIs.
  The existing memory leaf is already at its 100-rule budget; no existing
  memory rules were split or migrated merely to make capacity.
- The suspicious writer rule binds the published invalid stream to a hex
  decoder and follows its result through actual local helper returns into a
  file writer. It covers Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and C# source APIs.
  It requires no chosen filename, package marker, CVE name, or English prose.
- The hostile composite adds nearby real JPEG XL compressed-metadata and
  codestream tags. Its description deliberately says "with JPEG XL boxes";
  the rule proves output flow of malformed Brotli, plus container context,
  rather than claiming interprocedural proof of a particular box's argument.
- Generic brob/jxlc references live in data/format/container at notable severity.
- Added notable Python direct/streaming Brotli, .NET buffer/stream, and native
  source decoder calls in data/decompress/brotli. These do not claim that a
  decoder is vulnerable or that an input is attacker controlled. Python
  arbitrary aliases and custom wrappers are not universally resolved.
- The existing big-endian-u32-framing matcher fired on image box serialization.
  Moved its identical matcher and platform/type/confidence scope to
  data/codec::python-big-endian-u32-format; removed inherited T1573 attribution.
  Updated all four exact consumers (three local and one SOCKS composite).
  No behavioral ancestor-directory consumers were found. This preserves the
  exact observation while removing an unsupported networking classification.
- New JPEG XL container observations use an existing leaf. Its existing
  consumers select exact HEIF rules; no broad ancestor selectors were found.

Checks
- cleave facts captured builder source literals, calls, imports, value-flow
  graph and decoded strings in builder-facts.json. Raw-format facts are in
  raw-facts.json. No further hidden payload emerged from decoded strings.
- controls-final.json records passing Python reconstruction, a changed-marker
  Python variant, and a JavaScript port using Buffer.from/Buffer.concat.
- Eight benign/near-miss files under
  /usr/local/var/cyclotron/cleave/tests/fixtures/brotli-decoder/ have no
  suspicious/hostile findings: valid metadata, comments only, unused vector
  with unrelated output, compression mode, direct Python decompression, .NET
  stream and buffer decompression, and native C decompression.
- All five new decoder API observations fire on their corresponding controls.
- atomscan was run initially and after edits over testdata/. The sole actual
  sample meets the suspicious-tier floor with one suspicious malformed-stream
  writer and one hostile JPEG XL builder. acceptance-atomscan.json records the
  final scan. Ordinary capabilities are not counted toward the floor.
- This supports two attack findings, not 3-5 distinct hostile behaviors.
  No shell execution, exfiltration, persistence, or additional intent was
  invented to increase the count.

Remaining coverage gaps
- Original .NET staged payload, 23 MB ClickHouse body, and 534-byte Arrow input
  are not published at the supplied links. Their separate crash/hang vectors
  cannot be reconstructed faithfully from lengths or API names alone.
- Raw .br and .jxl bytes are classified as unknown by this engine and do not
  reach a format-scoped rule. An attempted raw-byte trait was removed after
  full-scan checks showed it ineffective; no raw binary coverage is claimed.
- The retained rules cover the documented stream layout with mutable literal
  bytes and padding, not every possible malformed Brotli bitstream. A changed
  block layout or opaque decode wrapper can evade static source matching.
- atomscan's model reports an existing v18/v21 feature-spec warning. Trait
  evidence and the acceptance floor are verified independently of ML scores.
  The generic source flow graph also reports its ordinary may-flow limitation;
  positive and unrelated-output controls confirm the required relationship.

Indicator ledger
- SHA256, PURLS, ENDPOINTS are intentionally empty: the article identifies no
  hostile file hash, malicious package coordinate, or hostile network endpoint.
- github.com hosts research and fixes. System.IO.Compression.Brotli is a .NET
  API/assembly identity, not a DNS hostname. clickhouse is a demonstration
  service name. None is a malicious endpoint.
- Upstream Brotli affected scopes (1.0.3 before 1.0.10, 1.1.0 before 1.1.1,
  1.2.0 before 1.2.1), pyarrow 26.0.0, .NET 10.0.13 and ClickHouse 26.10.2.103
  describe clean vulnerable software, not malicious distribution identities.
  No malicious source-package PURL is inferred from these version scopes.
- 0ed4268a4401abcb4472096340477cf4af7d1a2b is a fix commit ID, not a file hash.
  The linked .NET issue's library hash describes a clean vulnerable runtime;
  it is not an article-supplied malicious hash and is excluded.
